paras: The threatened lynching of James Hughes took place at St. Ignace, Michigan, in February 1888, when a crowd went for Hughes, a lumberman accused of stealing a half dollar from the eye of a dead man. Officers kept him from harm, and he was held for trial. Papers from California to Virginia carried the story as a real case of the old saying about a man mean enough to steal from a dead man's eyes.

On Tuesday, February 7, 1888, Watson Sherman, a young bridge carpenter, was killed while working on a new slip at St. Ignace, struck by a swinging pile. His badly injured body was taken to Mallett & Walker's undertaking rooms, where a silver half dollar was placed over one eye to hold the lid down.

According to the St. Ignace dispatch, Hughes loafed around the body and, when nobody was looking, took the coin and left a penny in its place. He was arrested at once and was reported to have pleaded guilty, saying he had been drinking and did not know what he was doing.

Accounts differ on where the crowd turned on him. The fuller version of the wire said that "enraged lumbermen in the neighborhood" made a rush for Hughes and would have lynched him had officers not taken him to jail. A special to the St. Louis Globe-Democrat instead placed the threat in the crowded court room, where spectators shouted "Lynch him!" and "Tar and feather the brute!" while the marshal kept watch over the prisoner. A shorter Virginia notice said only that the spectators at his examination "came near mobbing him."

Justice Ruthford held Hughes in $1,000 bail for trial at the next session of the Circuit Court. No arrests of anyone in the crowd were reported, and no report of Hughes's trial or its outcome was found.

The story reached the white press in two forms. The St. Ignace wire of February 8 ran in the Rock Island Argus as "Michigan's Meanest Thief" without any mention of a crowd, and the next day in the Sacramento Record-Union under "The Worst Yet" with the closing line about the lumbermen. Later in February the Globe-Democrat account, which called Hughes "the meanest man on earth," appeared in the Washington Critic, and uncredited copies ran in the Alexandria Gazette and the Shepherdstown Register, both of which placed St. Ignace in "Mo."

Every version made the theft the story and Hughes its villain. The threats against him served as color: the Record-Union credited the officers for preventing a lynching, while the Globe-Democrat quoted the spectators' cries without comment.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of James Hughes
bases: A crowd threatened to lynch Hughes, a prisoner accused of theft, and officers kept him from it (A2, A4); no one was killed, so this is an attempted or threatened lynching.
No one was killed: a crowd of lumbermen or courtroom spectators rushed at or shouted to lynch Hughes over the theft, but officers protected him and he was held for trial (A2, A3, A4).

Two independent texts, the St. Ignace wire (A2) and the Globe-Democrat special (A4), both report a crowd seeking to lynch Hughes, with A3 adding that spectators 'came near mobbing him'; they differ on the setting.

accounts.label: St. Ignace wire (Feb. 8)
accounts.gist: After his arrest and guilty plea, enraged lumbermen made a rush for Hughes and would have lynched him had officers not taken him to jail; a shorter version of the same wire omits the rush.

accounts.label: St. Louis Globe-Democrat special
accounts.gist: At his trial before Justice Ruthford, spectators in the crowded court room shouted to brain, tar and feather, or lynch Hughes, and the marshal guarded him; he was held for the Circuit Court.

framing.detail: Headlines like 'The Worst Yet' and 'A Low-Bred Creature Steals a Piece of Silver from a Corpse's Eye' condemned the thief; the threatened lynching was a closing line, with credit to the officers.

The Globe-Democrat story, retold under 'Coins From a Dead Man's Eyes' and reprinted as 'The Ideal Thief Appears' and 'The Meanest of All Thieves', called Hughes 'the meanest man on earth' and quoted the spectators' cries without comment.

versions.value: Lumbermen rushed Hughes after his arrest; officers took him to jail
Spectators shouted threats in the crowded court room at his examination; the marshal guarded him

conflicts.note: The two may describe different moments of the same day; neither text mentions the other scene.
The 'Mo.' reprints are uncredited copies of the Globe-Democrat text, which gives Michigan (A4); Michigan is the dateline of the wire.
